anchor_text: It was a handkerchief, an antique token My father gave my mother
summary: Othello now describes the handkerchief simply as his father's gift to his mother — a plain domestic inheritance — which flatly contradicts his earlier claim (3.4) that an Egyptian sorceress gave it to his mother and that it was woven by a sibyl. The two stories cannot both be true. Whether this is a mistake or deliberate inconsistency on Shakespeare's part, or a sign that Othello's earlier story was a frightening tale invented to control Desdemona, has been debated for centuries.

It also returns the prop to its real dramatic weight: it is his father's gift, a token of a marriage, now used to 'prove' the ruin of his own.

anchor_text: I will play the swan, And die in music
summary: The 'swan song' was a classical legend: the swan, supposedly silent throughout its life, sang one beautiful song as it was dying. Dying in music was considered a blessed, peaceful death.

Emilia's use of it here is deeply moving: she is dying in defence of her mistress and sings the very song Desdemona sang on the eve of her death.

anchor_text: It is a sword of Spain, the ice-brook's temper
summary: Spanish swords, especially those made at Toledo, were famous across Europe for their quality. 'The ice-brook's temper' means the blade has been hardened by quenching the hot steel in an icy mountain stream — a technique associated specifically with Toledo blades, which were said to be plunged into the cold waters of the Tagus or its tributaries. A well-tempered blade was the mark of a professional soldier.

'Temper' is the technical word for the hardening achieved by heating and rapidly cooling metal; 'ice-brook' specifies the cold-water quench that made the blade resilient. Othello's careful identification of this sword is part of his recovery of his identity as a soldier — 'I have another weapon in this chamber' — before he uses it on himself.

anchor_text: I look down towards his feet;--but that's a fable.-- If that thou be'st a devil, I cannot kill thee
summary: Othello looks at Iago's feet to see if he has the cloven hooves of the devil — and then dismisses that as a 'fable' (a folk-story, a superstition). In popular legend, the devil in human form could be identified by his animal feet: he could disguise everything about himself except his hooves. Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) describes the devil appearing in human form but with visible tell-tale feet. anchor_text: that demi-devil Why he hath thus ensnar'd my soul and body
summary: A 'demi-devil' is a half-devil — a being with demonic powers but who appears human. Othello is not just using an insult: he is genuinely asking how a human being could have done what Iago did, and concluding that only a partially supernatural evil could explain it. The question 'why' is the one Iago pointedly refuses to answer: 'Demand me nothing.' The unanswered question is the play's final horror.
detail: The idea that some people are literally half-demonic — born of a devil and a human woman — was part of early modern demonology. In The Tempest Caliban is called 'a devil, a born devil' (4.1) and Prospero says his mother was a witch. Iago is given no comparable supernatural origin, and that is precisely the problem: his evil is human. His silence before the demand for an explanation mirrors Satan's refusal to justify himself — compare Satan in Milton's Paradise Lost, which draws on the same tradition.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'demi-devil' n.: a half-devil; cf. Stuart Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997), on the early modern concept of diabolical human-devil offspring.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3388

OED s.v. 'demi-devil' n. is a real entry; Stuart Clark Thinking with Demons (1997) is a real and authoritative scholarly work on early modern demonology that discusses diabolical human-devil concepts.

The gloss is sound, but the detail that Iago 'never will speak word' is stated as part of the horror of unanswered 'why' is premature here — this annotation is on 'demi-devil' (TLN 3388), and Iago's silence is his next speech (TLN 3390), a separate annotation; the parallel to Milton's Satan is also a reach given that Paradise Lost postdates the play by six decades, but the core claim about Othello's genuine question and the demonological context is defensible.

anchor_text: Demand me nothing: what you know, you know: From this time forth I never will speak word
summary: Iago's last words — two sentences of absolute refusal — are among the most chilling exits in Shakespeare. He will not explain himself. Most dramatic villains confess their schemes when caught; Iago denies the audience (and Othello) the comprehension they want. His silence has been read as the ultimate assertion of power: to refuse to be understood is to remain the master of the situation even in defeat.
detail: The line has generated enormous critical commentary. Some readers see it as authentic Machiavellian defiance; others as a practical refusal to give evidence that could be used at trial; others still as evidence that Iago has no motive adequate to what he has done and knows it. Harold Bloom (Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human, 1998) argues Iago is 'motiveless malignity' (a phrase borrowed from Coleridge). Whatever its cause, the silence has the effect of making Iago a kind of abstract evil — less a person than a force — which is precisely what Othello's 'demi-devil' suggests.

sources.name: Coleridge on Shakespeare
sources.citation: S. T. Coleridge, Lectures on Shakespeare, 1818 (the phrase 'motiveless malignity'); cf. Harold Bloom, Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human (1998), ch. 21.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3390

Coleridge's 'motiveless malignity' phrase from his 1818 lecture notes is confirmed as real and accurately attributed; Harold Bloom Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human (1998) exists and discusses Iago as a central figure.

The identification of Iago's final silence as the play's central interpretive crux is mainstream; presenting Coleridge's 'motiveless malignity' with attribution is correct; the note that Bloom's use of the phrase is borrowed from Coleridge is accurate and important.

anchor_text: Speak of me as I am; nothing extenuate, Nor set down aught in malice
summary: 'Extenuate' means to lessen, mitigate, make something seem less serious — from Latin extenuare (to thin out, reduce). Othello asks Lodovico and Cassio, who will carry the report back to Venice, to describe him accurately: neither softening what he did nor distorting it with hostility. It is a request for honest history, made by a man who is about to write his own epitaph by suicide. The irony is that the self-description he then gives — 'one that loved not wisely but too well' — is itself a form of extenuating.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'extenuate' v. 3: to lessen the seeming gravity of, to palliate; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'extenuate.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3434
OED s.v. 'extenuate' v.3 (to lessen the seeming gravity of) and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon are real sources accurately supporting the definition given.

The gloss of 'extenuate' is accurate; the ironic observation that 'loved not wisely but too well' is itself a form of extenuating is a well-established critical point (Leavis, Eliot) and is justified here.

anchor_text: Of one that loved not wisely, but too well; Of one not easily jealous, but, being wrought, Perplex'd in the extreme
summary: Othello constructs his own epitaph in a series of antitheses: 'not wisely but too well,' 'not easily jealous but, being wrought, perplex'd in the extreme.' Each phrase admits a fault while insisting on the quality that makes it understandable — he loved deeply, he was not naturally suspicious. Editors have debated whether this self-portrait is honest self-knowledge or a final act of self-romanticising that avoids full responsibility. 'Perplex'd' means utterly confused, distracted beyond reason.
detail: F. R. Leavis, in 'Diabolic Intellect and the Noble Hero' (1952), argued this speech is self-deception — that Othello is already converting his crime into a story that flatters him. T. S. Eliot in 'Shakespeare and the Stoicism of Seneca' (1927) made the same charge: Othello is 'cheering himself up.' Others (including Honigmann) read the speech as genuinely moving in its acknowledgment of failure. The antitheses at least show a man trying to face the truth: he admits he was 'perplex'd,' manipulated ('wrought'), and fatally excessive in love.

sources.name: Honigmann, ed., Othello
sources.citation: E. A. J. Honigmann, ed., Othello, Arden Shakespeare, 3rd series (1997), note to 5.2.340-345; T. S. Eliot, 'Shakespeare and the Stoicism of Seneca' (1927).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3436

Honigmann Arden 1997 note to 5.2.340-345 is a real citation; T. S. Eliot 'Shakespeare and the Stoicism of Seneca' (1927) is a confirmed real essay that argues Othello is 'cheering himself up' — accurately summarised.

The annotation fairly presents both the self-romanticising reading (Leavis, Eliot) and the sympathetic reading (Honigmann) without collapsing into either; 'perplex'd' as thoroughly confused/distracted is correct.

anchor_text: Like the base Judean, threw a pearl away Richer than all his tribe
summary: Othello compares himself to a 'base Judean' who threw away a pearl worth more than his whole people. Most editors read 'Judean' as a reference to Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus — the most precious person imaginable — for thirty pieces of silver. (Some editions print 'Indian' instead, based on a variant in the Quarto text.) If 'Judean' is right, the image frames Desdemona as the pearl of great price and Othello as her betrayer.
detail: The Folio text reads 'Iudean'; the Quarto of 1622 reads 'Indian.' Both are plausible: 'Judean' (Judas Iscariot, who betrayed his lord) fits the religious register of the rest of the speech — hell-fire, damnation, the Last Judgment — and the Geneva Bible Matthew 13:45-46 speaks of 'a marchant man that sought goodly pearles, who when he had found one pearle of great price, went and sold all that he had.' 'Indian' (proverbially ignorant of the value of pearls) is also defended. Honigmann and Neill both favour 'Judean.' Either way Othello is calling himself the destroyer of what he most valued.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 13:45-46 (Geneva 1599): the pearl of great price; Judas Iscariot as the betrayer: Matthew 26:14-16, 27:3-10. See Honigmann, ed., Othello, Arden Shakespeare, 3rd series (1997), note to 5.2.346-347.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3439

The annotation correctly flags the Folio/Quarto textual crux ('Iudean' vs. 'Indian'), presents both readings fairly, notes the biblical 'pearl of great price' parallel (Matthew 13:45-46), and assigns medium confidence — all appropriate; Judas Iscariot as the referent for 'Judean' is the mainstream Folio-based reading.

anchor_text: the Arabian trees Their medicinal gum
summary: Arabia was famous in antiquity and the Renaissance for producing aromatic gum-resins such as frankincense, myrrh, and bdellium — the 'medicinal gum' exuded from desert trees. The gum dripping from the trees was compared to tears. Othello is saying his tears fall like the slow, precious drops that ooze from the Arabian spice trees — involuntary, rare, and carrying a kind of sacred weight. The image comes from Pliny and was current in English writing about Arabia.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 12.30-35 (the frankincense country and the frankincense and myrrh trees of Arabia and their exuded gums), trans. Philemon Holland (London, 1601).

anchor_text: in Aleppo once, Where a malignant and a turban'd Turk Beat a Venetian and traduc'd the state, I took by the throat the circumcised dog And smote him--thus
summary: Othello recounts killing a Turkish enemy at Aleppo — and then stabs himself, the sword turning on the man who acted against Venice. The story of the Turk is a trap: as he speaks of punishing the enemy of Venice who 'traduc'd' (slandered, dishonoured) the state, he enacts the punishment on himself. He has become his own enemy — the one who dishonoured Venice, who betrayed the state's trust. 'Circumcised' was a contemptuous term for a Muslim; 'turban'd' the visual marker of the Ottoman enemy.
detail: Aleppo was a major Ottoman trading city in Syria, where Venetian merchants operated under Ottoman authority. A Venetian consul or merchant beaten by a Turk was an act of geopolitical humiliation; the commander who executed the offender was a servant of Venetian honour. By recasting himself in that role at the moment of suicide, Othello both condemns himself as the enemy of Venice and executes the sentence — the soldier still in command of himself even as he destroys himself. The Folio stage direction reads simply 'Stabs himself.'

sources.name: Cyprus and the Ottoman threat
sources.citation: Richard Knolles, The Generall Historie of the Turkes (London, 1603), on Ottoman power in the eastern Mediterranean and Venetian relations; cf. the reference card on Cyprus and the Ottoman threat.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3444
Richard Knolles The Generall Historie of the Turkes (London, 1603) is a confirmed real publication whose date and place match the citation.

The trap-structure of the Aleppo story — Othello describing the punishment of an enemy of Venice and enacting it on himself — is the mainstream reading and is plainly supported by the stage direction 'Stabs himself'; the historical context of Venetian merchants in Ottoman Aleppo is accurate.

anchor_text: I kiss'd thee ere I kill'd thee:--no way but this, Killing myself, to die upon a kiss
summary: Othello's last words are a couplet built on the paradox of love and death: 'kiss'd / kill'd', 'killing myself / die upon a kiss.' The line fuses the two acts — the kiss in the opening of the scene (TLN 3059-3062) and the killing — and closes the scene where it began: with Othello over Desdemona's body, kissing her. The stage direction 'Falling upon Desdemona' completes the image. Death and love are literally joined at the moment he falls.
detail: The Italian word 'morire' (to die) also meant in Renaissance usage to experience sexual ecstasy, and critics have read the dying kiss as the consummation of a marriage that was never peacefully consummated in Cyprus. Whether or not this bawdy layer is active, the theatrical effect is clear: Othello, who began the scene trying to sacrifice Desdemona without 'scar that whiter skin,' ends by making himself inseparable from her. The line has been widely read as one of the most formally perfect closing couplets in Shakespeare's tragic canon.

sources.name: Neill, ed., Othello
sources.citation: Michael Neill, ed., Othello, Oxford Shakespeare (2006), note to 5.2.356-357; on the Renaissance double sense of 'die': Gordon Williams, A Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (1997), s.v. 'die.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3451

The formal analysis of 'kiss'd/kill'd' and the closing-where-it-began structure is sound; the note on the Renaissance 'die' double sense (sexual ecstasy) is correctly hedged as a possible layer rather than asserted as primary, which is the responsible approach.

anchor_text: O Spartan dog, More fell than anguish, hunger, or the sea
summary: Lodovico calls Iago a 'Spartan dog' — a breed known for being fierce, lean, and relentless in pursuit, used for hunting. The Spartans were proverbially austere, hard, and merciless. Calling Iago a Spartan hunting-dog compares him to an animal that tracks and destroys without pity or regret. 'Fell' means savage, cruel.
detail: Spartan hounds were mentioned by classical authors — Xenophon (On Hunting 10) and Ovid (Metamorphoses 3.208-224, the hunting dogs of Actaeon) — as among the best and most ferocious hunting breeds. The comparison reduces Iago from a person to a predatory animal at the last, echoing the many animal images applied to him throughout the play. 'More fell than anguish, hunger, or the sea' names three great causes of pain that Iago surpasses: the image caps the play's long sequence of comparisons between Iago and inhuman forces.

sources.name: Xenophon, On Hunting
sources.citation: Xenophon, On Hunting (Cynegeticus) 10 (on Spartan hounds and their qualities); Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.206-225 (the hunting-dogs of Actaeon).
